findings.title: Model re-download permanently removes imported custom voices
findings.evidence: download_model deletes the entire existing model_dir with shutil.rmtree before moving the downloaded snapshot. The new server stores imported user styles at get_cache_dir(model)/custom_styles by default (server/styles_store.py:58). CLI cmd_download invokes this unconditionally (cli.py:222-223).
findings.impact: After importing a custom voice, running the documented supertonic download command (or auto-repair after any ONNX module is missing) deletes those user voice files without warning or recovery. Even user-supplied model_dir contents are deleted. External originals/backups remain intact; a SUPERTONIC_CUSTOM_STYLES_DIR outside the model/cache directory avoids this deletion.
findings.recommendation: Keep user-imported styles outside the replaceable downloaded model directory, or preserve and restore the custom_styles directory while atomically replacing only managed model assets. Retain a backup until replacement succeeds.
findings.validation: Confirmed in a TemporaryDirectory using real loader.download_model and mocked huggingface_hub.snapshot_download: seeded custom_styles/my_voice.json existed before the call and was absent afterwards. No live user data touched. Reproducer: /workspace/review/repro_supertonic.py. Independently confirmed via the real CLI download and auto-download repair paths with temporary valid custom-style storage; only model initialization/HuggingFace download were mocked.
findings.classification: Confirmed through the validation described below

findings.title: Batch voice defaults silently select M1 instead
findings.evidence: BatchItem.voice defaults to nonempty M1. routes.py:365 chooses item.voice before defaults.voice, so an omitted item voice never inherits defaults.voice.
findings.impact: A valid batch request with defaults.voice=F1 and items containing only text returns audio from M1, silently using the wrong requested voice.
findings.recommendation: Make BatchItem.voice optional with a None default, then resolve item voice -> defaults.voice -> M1 in the route. Add a test for omitted item voice plus batch default and an explicit item override.
findings.validation: Confirmed through the real FastAPI app/TestClient with FakeTTS: POST /v1/tts/batch using defaults.voice=F1 returned HTTP 200, but the synthesizer received M1. Reproducer saved.
findings.classification: Confirmed through the validation described below

findings.title: Chunked JSON imports bypass the 1 MiB request limit
findings.evidence: StyleImportSizeLimit passes requests without Content-Length (app.py:65-67). The JSON branch then calls request.json() without a bounded read; unlike the file branch, it never checks MAX_STYLE_IMPORT_BYTES. FastAPI multipart dependencies may also buffer/spool before handler file.read, so enforcing the actual incoming ASGI byte count is preferable.
findings.impact: A reachable HTTP client can submit arbitrarily large JSON uploads to a server that claims a 1 MiB cap, causing unbounded body buffering and parsing. The default server is loopback-only; risk grows when configured for a LAN/service binding.
findings.recommendation: Enforce a cumulative receive-byte limit in the ASGI middleware for all import content types, independent of Content-Length, and reject oversized bodies before parsing.
findings.validation: Confirmed via TestClient content iterator (Transfer-Encoding chunked): 1,048,704-byte JSON with a valid small style plus an ignored large field was accepted with HTTP 200. No large resource-exhaustion payload was used.
findings.classification: Confirmed through the validation described below

findings.title: Long individual sentences bypass max_chunk_length
findings.evidence: When a sentence exceeds max_len, the function assigns it unchanged to current_chunk. There is no fallback split at words/characters; sentence splitting only recognizes ASCII .!? followed by whitespace.
findings.impact: The documented maximum chunk length is not enforced for pasted unpunctuated text or Japanese text with normal sentence punctuation. These inputs are sent as one large model inference despite the selected limit. Exact memory/latency impact was not measured.
findings.recommendation: After sentence splitting, split overlong sentences at word boundaries, with a bounded character fallback for text without spaces, including Unicode punctuation handling.
findings.validation: Confirmed real chunk_text('word '*400, max_len=300) returns one chunk of 1,999 characters. Same bug exists in supertonic/py/helper.py:418-427.
findings.classification: Confirmed through the validation described below

findings.title: Chunked JSON imports bypass the 1 MiB request limit
findings.evidence: StyleImportSizeLimit passes requests without Content-Length (app.py:65-67). The JSON branch then calls request.json() without a bounded read; unlike the file branch, it never checks MAX_STYLE_IMPORT_BYTES. FastAPI multipart dependencies may also buffer/spool before handler file.read, so enforcing the actual incoming ASGI byte count is preferable.
findings.impact: A reachable HTTP client can submit arbitrarily large JSON uploads to a server that claims a 1 MiB cap, causing unbounded body buffering and parsing. The default server is loopback-only; risk grows when configured for a LAN/service binding.
findings.recommendation: Enforce a cumulative receive-byte limit in the ASGI middleware for all import content types, independent of Content-Length, and reject oversized bodies before parsing.
findings.validation: Confirmed via TestClient content iterator (Transfer-Encoding chunked): 1,048,704-byte JSON with a valid small style plus an ignored large field was accepted with HTTP 200. No large resource-exhaustion payload was used.
repair_steps: Retain the Content-Length preflight for early rejection, but count actual body bytes as the import request is received.

At a 1 MiB limit, a simple bounded pre-read with replay to the downstream app can be easier to reason about than letting FastAPI consume an unbounded stream; reject at limit+1 before JSON/multipart parsing.
Alternatively wrap ASGI receive with a counting boundary and a dedicated overflow control path; ensure the response is sent once and no success response can be started after overflow.
Enforce the same byte definition for JSON and multipart including the policy on multipart envelope overhead. Handle split messages and client disconnect without retaining files or partial styles.
Return the existing OpenAI-shaped 413 payload_too_large envelope; leave normal route behavior unchanged.
invariants: No import path buffers/parses more than the stated cumulative body limit before rejection.
Content-Length absence, understated length, different chunk sizes and content type do not bypass the limit.
Rejected imports do not create or overwrite a custom style file.
Other routes and non-HTTP ASGI events remain unaffected by this narrowly scoped limit.
acceptance_criteria: The recorded 1,048,704-byte JSON iterator request returns 413 rather than 200.
Under-limit known-length and chunked JSON/multipart imports still work.
An exactly-at-limit request follows a documented inclusive rule; limit+1 rejects.
An over-limit body does not reach the style save operation or leave disk-spooled upload residue owned by the application.
regression_scenarios: Content-Length missing/invalid/over-limit
Body arrives as one chunk and many small chunks
Multipart envelope overhead and a file straddling limit
JSON with large ignored fields
Disconnect mid-request
Rejected overwrite leaves existing custom style intact
risks: ASGI middleware ordering and receive replay can break multipart parsing or duplicate responses if not tested.
A body-counting fix is a specific request boundary; it does not add authentication, rate limits or global resource controls.
Claims about multipart parser buffering were source-informed; only the JSON bypass was dynamically demonstrated.
findings.rollback: Revert middleware changes if valid clients break, retain loopback-only exposure and enforce an actual byte cap in an upstream proxy until a corrected implementation is accepted. A limit-only rollback needs no data migration.

findings.evidence: When a sentence exceeds max_len, the function assigns it unchanged to current_chunk. There is no fallback split at words/characters; sentence splitting only recognizes ASCII .!? followed by whitespace.
findings.impact: The documented maximum chunk length is not enforced for pasted unpunctuated text or Japanese text with normal sentence punctuation. These inputs are sent as one large model inference despite the selected limit. Exact memory/latency impact was not measured.

repair_steps: Define maximum length over Python Unicode characters and preserve the existing paragraph/sentence ordering and abbreviation rules.
For a sentence longer than max_len, split at available whitespace boundaries; if an individual span still exceeds the limit, split it by bounded character positions.
Recognize common Unicode sentence punctuation so Japanese text can retain useful boundaries; hard fallback must still enforce the maximum when punctuation/whitespace is absent.
Return nonempty bounded chunks without dropping, reordering or duplicating input text. Preserve the documented whitespace-normalization behavior.

Add regressions for unpunctuated words, one long word, Japanese text without spaces, Korean text, abbreviations and exact limits. Coordinate behavior with the sibling Python implementation without introducing a cross-repository runtime dependency.
invariants: Every returned chunk is nonempty and has len(chunk) <= configured max_len.
Original meaningful characters retain order and are emitted exactly once.
Empty/whitespace input and existing sentence/paragraph behavior remain defined.
Minimum-limit validation remains consistent with the public SDK or example contract.
